CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion ### Abstract Exact _k_-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near- duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call CertEx. Specifically, CertEx stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that CertEx returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, CertEx is exact for every query at 7.1\(\times\) to 18.0\(\times\) the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 (8.8\(\times\) to 11.8\(\times\) on an A100) and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact. ### 1 Introduction Exact kNN search over large datasets of visual features is a basic operation whose errors propagate into the tasks built on top of it. For instance, image retrieval ranks database descriptors such as SIFT [42] by their distance to a query descriptor, so that a missed neighbor removes a relevant image from the ranked list. Similarly, near-duplicate detection in web-scale training corpora such as LAION [58] compares every image embedding with its nearest neighbors [54], so that a missed neighbor keeps a duplicate pair in the training data. Likewise, the kNN classifier that evaluates self- supervised representations [12, 50, 70] reports the search error together with the quality of the representation whenever its neighbors are approximate. Moreover, LLMs and agents increasingly read long contexts and memories by nearest- neighbor search [4, 11, 34, 38, 39, 67, 69, 71], so that a missed neighbor drops a relevant memory. Finally, every benchmark of approximate search measures recall against exact neighbors and therefore inherits any error of the exhaustive search that computes them. Existing systems respond to the cost of exact search in two ways, both of which leave a gap. First, exhaustive search on GPUs [18, 35] computes every query-to-vector distance at full precision. The throughput of exhaustive search is therefore bounded by one full-precision distance per vector, and its capacity is bounded by device memory, which must hold every vector at full precision. Second, approximate indexes based on quantization [22, 28, 37] or proximity graphs [43, 49, 63] are much faster. However, these indexes trade recall for speed by design and rely on an index that must be built before the first query and repaired when the dataset changes [74]. Practitioners therefore choose between exact results at high cost and fast results whose errors are not controlled per query. To close this gap, we follow the division of labor in human vision: the periphery examines the whole visual field in parallel at low resolution, whereas high resolution is spent only on the few locations that attention selects [13, 65]. Transferred to kNN search, this principle examines every database vector at low precision in one parallel pass and spends full precision only on the few vectors that the pass cannot exclude. However, a low-precision distance is not exact. Consequently, unless every low-precision decision is certified to be conservative, the pass loses neighbors in the same way as an approximate index. We address this difficulty with a principle that we call _certified exclusion_: a test may run in any arithmetic as long as it never excludes a vector within the threshold, so that verifying the kept vectors yields the exact neighbors. We realize this principle in an exact search method that we call CertEx. Specifically, CertEx stores a lower-bounding projection of every vector in half precision, together with four coordinates that fold the rounding and accumulation errors [10, 29] of the tensor-core dot product into the product itself. As a result, one dot product and one comparison per vector decide whether the vector can still be a neighbor, without a top-_k_ selection and without a false dismissal. For instance, Figure 1(a) follows one text query through CertEx: the certified test keeps 274 of the 1,281,167 ImageNet [15] training images, from which the fovea returns the exact best matches. By comparison, CAGRA [49] loses the best matching image for the two prompts of Figure 1(b), even at its most accurate configuration. Beyond these examples, CertEx returns exact results on one H100 GPU with 7.1\(\times\) to 18.0\(\times\) the throughput of the fastest cuVS [47] fp32 configuration on sixteen datasets, with a speedup that grows with the database size. CertEx also outperforms the GPU indexes IVF-Flat [62], IVF-PQ [37], IVF-RaBitQ [22], and CAGRA [49] whenever every query must be exact.

In summary, we make three contributions.

• We propose certified exclusion, a new principle for exact search that replaces the ranking of all _N_ vectors by one keep-or-exclude decision per vector. Because the decision never excludes a vector within the threshold, even when it runs in half precision, verifying only the kept vectors returns the exact neighbors.<tbc>

• We design CertEx as an exact kNN method that realizes certified exclusion on GPU tensor cores [10]. We call its data structure the retina, which is a single half-precision matrix with one row per database vector. Each row holds a lower-bounding projection of one vector and four coordinates of a rounding certificate. We prove that its one-pass tensor-core test never discards a true neighbor, answers range queries and similarity self-joins (all pairs within a radius) exactly, and keeps survivors between two balls whose gap shrinks as the principal coordinates capture more of the data.<tbc>

• We evaluate CertEx on sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, including the embeddings of seven vi<tbc>

sion encoders such as CLIP [56], DINOv2 [50], and DINOv3 [61]. CertEx answers every query exactly at 7.1\(\times\) to 18.0\(\times\) the throughput of the fastest exhaustive search of NVIDIA cuVS [47] and is faster than IVF-Flat [62], IVF-PQ [37], IVF-RaBitQ [22], and CAGRA [49] whenever every query must be exact. On the 12.8M web images of DataComp [21], CertEx is exact for every query and finds all 31.4 billion duplicate pairs, which makes exact deduplication [1] practical at web scale.

## 2 Related Work

### Exact search with lower bounds.

Exact methods avoid computing every distance by excluding the vectors whose lower bound exceeds the current neighbor distance. For instance, the k-d tree [7] and the cover tree [9] bound whole regions, whereas AESA [66] bounds single points by the triangle inequality with precomputed pivots. However, the pruning power of such bounds decays with the dimension [8, 68]. The GEMINI framework [19] therefore moves the bound into a contractive feature space with a proof of no false dismissal, which the VA-file [68] turns into a sequential scan of compact approximations. In contrast, random projections preserve distances only up to a distortion factor [36] and support only approximate hashing [14, 30], whereas exhaustive GPU search [24, 35] avoids bounds altogether. In our terms, GEMINI and the VA-file are certified exclusion tests in full precision whose survivors are still ranked against a running candidate set; in contrast, CertEx certifies a half-precision tensor-core decision inside the same product and replaces the ranking by one comparison per vector.

### Approximate indexes.

Approximate indexes trade exactness for fewer examined vectors. Specifically, product quantization [6, 25, 28, 37] compresses vectors and probes a few partitions, to which RaBitQ [22, 23] adds a probabilistic error bound. In addition, FLANN [46] automates the choice<tbc>

Benchmarks \[5, 60\] accordingly rank these methods by recall at a given throughput, whereas CertEx examines every vector and returns exact results.

#### Nearest neighbors in visual recognition.

Visual recognition uses nearest neighbors as a component whose errors enter the task metric. For instance, object retrieval \[3, 32, 53, 62\] is evaluated against exhaustive ground truth \[55\]. Similarly, copy detection \[17, 54\] and dataset curation \[1, 21\] remove near and semantic duplicates from web-scale corpora. In representation learning, weighted kNN classifiers evaluate self-supervised representations \[12, 50, 61\]. Retrieval-augmented classification \[41\] even feeds the retrieved neighbors into the model. In practice, these pipelines obtain their neighbors from approximate indexes, cluster-restricted comparisons, or kNN graphs of fixed degree. In contrast, CertEx returns exact neighbors faster than exhaustive search and answers deduplication with an exact similarity self-join (Section 3.6).

#### Foveation and certified low-precision arithmetic.

Vision models allocate resolution unevenly, for instance through recurrent glimpses \[45\], foveal-peripheral segmentation \[2\], or foveated rendering \[27, 31\]. Numerical computing allocates precision in the same way, for instance in mixed-precision training \[44\]. Computational geometry goes further: its floating-point filters evaluate a predicate in fast arithmetic together with an error bound \[10, 29\] and fall back to exact arithmetic only near zero \[20, 59\]. Following this idea, CertEx folds the error bound into the same half- precision product, so that every low-precision decision of CertEx carries a proof of no false dismissal, unlike approximate foveation.

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 Overview

Exact kNN search must examine all _N_ database vectors, although only the few vectors near the query need full precision. Human vision solves the same problem by dividing its work between two parts of the retina \[13\] (Figure 2(a)): the periphery covers the whole scene at low resolution, whereas the fovea sees only one spot at full resolution. Our exact kNN method divides its work in the same way (Figure 2(b)). We call this method CertEx, which stands for certified exclusion.

The left half of Figure 2(b) shows the retina of CertEx, which stores one half-precision vector \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) for each of the _N_ database vectors **x**. We call \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) the _retina vector_ of **x**. The first part of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) keeps a few principal coordinates of **x** and summarizes the rest by one norm. We call this part the _lifted projection_ of **x** (Section 3.3). The inner product of two lifted projections determines a lower bound on the distance between their vectors. Although half precision is the fastest arithmetic of GPU tensor cores \[10\], rounding to half precision can overestimate the distance of a true neighbor. To guard against this error, the second part of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) records how large the rounding error of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) can be. We call this part the _certificate_ of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). With the certificate, the test excludes a vector only if the vector would be excluded even under the worst possible rounding. Moreover, the tensor cores evaluate this worst case within the same product (Section 3.4). Concretely, a tensor-core pass over the retina keeps a vector **x** only if \(\langle\hat{\mathbf{q}},\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rangle\ge\theta(\mathbf{q})\), where the retina vector \(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\) encodes the query **q** in the same form as \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and the threshold \(\theta(\mathbf{q})\) follows from an upper bound _U_ on the distance of the _k_-th nearest neighbor (Section 3.5). Because _U_ is needed before the pass, CertEx obtains it from a few sampled vectors. The test of each vector therefore depends on no other database vector, so that one pass over the retina decides all _N_ vectors without ranking them. We call this pass the _retina pass_. ## 3.2 Certified Exclusion

Consider a database \(\mathcal{X}:=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_N\}\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) and a query \(\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^D\). Exact kNN search returns the index set \(\mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{q}):=argmin_{\mathcal{S}\subseteq[N],|\mathcal{S}|=k}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}_i\|\), whose farthest member lies at the distance _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) from **q**. However, computing N_<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) requires exact distances only for the vectors that may be neighbors. Definition 1 therefore formalizes what a test that excludes the other vectors must guarantee, whatever arithmetic it uses.

**Definition 1** (Certified exclusion)**.** A test \(T(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x},U)\in\{\text{keep},\text{exclude}\}\) is a _certified exclusion test_ if its computed output keeps every vector **x** with \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|\le U\), for every query **q**, vector **x**, and threshold \(U\ge 0\).

Definition 1 constrains only the direction of the errors of a test. Specifically, a certified exclusion test may keep a vector farther than _U_ at the cost of one exact distance, but it never excludes a vector within _U_.

**Proposition 1** (Exact search by certified exclusion)**.** _For a certified exclusion test T and a threshold_ \(U\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\)_, the k vectors with the smallest exact distances among the vectors that T keeps form_ N_<sub>k</sub>_(**q**).

_Proof._ Every \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{q})\) satisfies \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|\le r_k(\mathbf{q})\le U\) and is therefore kept by Definition 1. The _k_ smallest exact distances among a superset of N_<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) are the _k_ smallest over X.

## 3.3 Lifted Lower Bound

Proposition 1 leaves open which certified exclusion test to use. CertEx needs a test that reads few bytes, because the retina pass reads every database vector and its cost grows with the number of bytes per vector. CertEx therefore keeps a few principal coordinates of each vector and one more coordinate that summarizes the rest, which together still give a lower bound on the distance. Specifically, consider a center \(\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^D\) and a matrix \(\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times D}\) whose orthonormal rows are the _m_ leading principal directions of a sample of X. We call _m_ the _width_ of the retina. The _lifted projection_ of a vector keeps its _m_ principal coordinates and summarizes the remaining _D-m_ coordinates by their norm:

\(\ell(\mathbf{x}):=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}) \\
\|(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c})\|
\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1}.\) (1)

**Proposition 2** (Lower bound)**.** _For all_ \(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^D\), \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|\).

_Proof._ The entry (_i,j_) of \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top\) is the inner product of rows _i_ and _j_ of **V**, which is 1 for _i=j_ and 0 otherwise because the rows are orthonormal. Hence \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top=\mathbf{I}_m\). We write \(\unknown:=\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}\) and prove the claim in five steps.

Step 1 splits the centered vectors. We define **u**:=**q**-**c**, **v**:=**x**-**c**, \(\mathbf{u}_1:=\unknown\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{u}_2:=\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}_1\), \(\mathbf{v}_1:=\unknown\mathbf{v}\), and \(\mathbf{v}_2:=\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}_1\). Two facts follow. First, with \(\mathbf{a}:=\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{R}^m\),

\(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{a}.\) (2)

Second, since \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top=\mathbf{I}_m\),

\(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}_2=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}\) (3)

and likewise **Vv**<sub>2</sub>=**0**.

Step 2 writes the lifted projections in these parts. Eq. (1) applied to **q** reads \(\ell(\mathbf{q})=[\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u};\|(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})\mathbf{u}\|]\), because **q**-**c**=**u**. Its first block is **Vu**=**V**(**u**<sub>1</sub>+**u**<sub>2</sub>)=**Vu**<sub>1</sub>+**Vu**<sub>2</sub>=**Vu**<sub>1</sub> by Eq. (3). Its last coordinate is \(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\), because \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}-\unknown\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{u}_2\). The same computation for **x** gives

\(\ell(\mathbf{q})=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}_1 \\
\|\mathbf{u}_2\|
\end{array}\right],\ell(\mathbf{x})=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{V}\mathbf{v}_1 \\
\|\mathbf{v}_2\|
\end{array}\right],\)

and subtracting the two gives

\(\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1) \\
\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|
\end{array}\right].\)

The squared norm of a stacked vector is the sum of the squared norms of its blocks, so that

\(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2=\|\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1)\|^2+(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2.\) (4)

Step 3 shows that **V** keeps the norm of **u**<sub>1</sub>-**v**<sub>1</sub>. By Eq. (2), \(\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{a}\) and \(\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2=\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{a}=\|\mathbf{a}\|^2\). Hence

\(\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2=\|\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1)\|^2.\) (5)

Step 4 applies the Pythagorean theorem. The center cancels in the difference, **q**-**x**=(**q**-**c**)-(**x**-**c**)=**u**-**v**, which splits as **y**+**z** with **y**:=**u**<sub>1</sub>-**v**<sub>1</sub> and **z**:=**u**<sub>2</sub>-**v**<sub>2</sub>. By Eqs. (2) and (3), the two parts are orthogonal:

\(\langle\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{a},\mathbf{z}\rangle=\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{a}^\top(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{V}\mathbf{v}_2)=0.\)

Expanding \(\|\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}\|^2=\|\mathbf{y}\|^2+2\langle\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}\rangle+\|\mathbf{z}\|^2\) therefore gives

\(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2=\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2+\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|^2.\) (6)

Step 5 applies the reverse triangle inequality. The triangle inequality gives \(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\le\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|+\|\mathbf{v}_2\|\) and \(\|\mathbf{v}_2\|\le\)<tbc>

\(\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|+\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\), so that \(\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|\ge\|\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|\). Squaring both nonnegative sides gives

\(\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\ge(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2.\) (7)

Combining the four relations,

\(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2=^{(6)}\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2+\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\ge^{(7)}\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2+(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2=^{(5)}\|\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1)\|^2+(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2=^{(4)}\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2.\)

Taking the square root of both nonnegative sides proves the claim.

Proposition 2 turns the lifted projection into an exclusion test. Specifically, if \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|>U\), then \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|>U\) as well, so that excluding **x** never removes a vector within _U_. However, the test must take a form that tensor cores evaluate quickly. This form is an inner product, because tensor cores multiply matrices and thus compute the inner products of many pairs of vectors at once. We therefore rewrite the test in terms of one inner product per pair. To this end, expanding the squared norm of a difference with \(a(\mathbf{x}):=\|\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2\) gives

\(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2=a(\mathbf{q})+a(\mathbf{x})-2\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle.\) (8)

Since both sides of the test \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\le U\) are nonnegative, the test holds exactly when the squared test holds. By Eq. (8), the squared test reads

\(a(\mathbf{q})+a(\mathbf{x})-2\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle\le U^2.\)

Moving the inner product to the right-hand side and _U_<sup>2</sup> to the left-hand side gives \(a(\mathbf{q})+a(\mathbf{x})-U^2\le 2\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle\). Dividing by 2 and moving _a_(**x**)/2 to the right-hand side finally gives the equivalent test

\(\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle-\frac{a(\mathbf{x})}{2}\ge\frac{a(\mathbf{q})-U^2}{2}.\) (9)

In this form, the right-hand side depends only on the query, so that CertEx computes it once per query. Similarly, on the left-hand side, _a_(**x**) depends only on the database vector and is computed once when the retina is built. The test of one pair therefore costs one inner product and one comparison, so that one matrix product on the tensor cores tests all pairs.

## 3.4 Certified Half-Precision Retina

To evaluate Eq. (9) for all vectors in one tensor-core pass, CertEx stores each lifted projection in half precision inside<tbc>

<tbc>its retina vector. However, rounding to half precision may underestimate the inner product, which overestimates the bound and can discard a true neighbor. To bound this effect, denote by \(\tilde{\ell}(\cdot)\) the rounding of \(\ell(\cdot)\) to the nearest half- precision numbers and by \(\delta(\cdot):=\|\ell(\cdot)-\tilde{\ell}(\cdot)\|\) its rounding error. Splitting the inner product into its rounded part and two error terms and applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to the error terms gives

\(\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle\le\langle\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q}),\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\rangle+\delta(\mathbf{q})\|\ell(\mathbf{x})\|+\|\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q})\|\delta(\mathbf{x}).\text{(10)}\)

Eq. (10) follows from the exact split

\(\langle\ell(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle=\langle\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q}),\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\rangle+\langle\ell(\mathbf{q})-\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})\rangle+\langle\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q}),\ell(\mathbf{x})-\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\rangle,\)

since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the last two terms by \(\delta(\mathbf{q})\|\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\) and \(\|\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q})\|\delta(\mathbf{x})\). A second error arises in the tensor cores, which multiply half-precision operands exactly but accumulate the products in fp32. This accumulation adds an error of at most \(\gamma\) times the sum of the absolute products, where \(\gamma\) depends only on the padded length _L_ of the retina vectors \[10, 29\].

CertEx folds both error terms into the same dot product, in the manner of floating-point filters \[59\]. Specifically, each database retina vector \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) appends four coordinates to \(\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\), which form its certificate: upper bounds <o>_n_</o><sub>**x**</sub> on \(\|\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\) and <o>_e_</o><sub>**x**</sub> on the rounding error \(\delta(\mathbf{x})\) plus an accumulation term, and a high part _h_<sub>**x**</sub> and a low part _l_<sub>**x**</sub> of _a_(**x**)/2 (the bars mark upper bounds). Correspondingly, the retina vector \(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\) of a query appends an upper bound <o>_e_</o><sub>**q**</sub> on \(\delta(\mathbf{q})\), an upper bound <o>_n_</o><sub>**q**</sub> on \(\|\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q})\|\), a coefficient \(1-\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\) slightly larger than \(\gamma\), and a one. The two retina vectors thus read

\(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^\top=[\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})^\top,\overline{n_\mathbf{x}},\overline{e_\mathbf{x}},-h_\mathbf{x},-l_\mathbf{x}],\hat{\mathbf{q}}^\top=[\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q})^\top,\overline{e_\mathbf{q}},\overline{n_\mathbf{q}},1-\varepsilon,1],\)

where the columns show which coordinates multiply each other. Denote by _P_ the exact inner product of \(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). By construction,

\(P=\langle\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{q}),\tilde{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\rangle+\overline{e_\mathbf{q}}\overline{n_\mathbf{x}}+\overline{n_\mathbf{q}}\overline{e_\mathbf{x}}-(1-\varepsilon)h_\mathbf{x}-l_\mathbf{x}.\) (11)

In Eq. (11), the products <o>_e_</o><sub>**q**</sub><o>_n_</o><sub>**x**</sub> and <o>_n_</o><sub>**q**</sub><o>_e_</sub><sub>**x**</sub> bound the two error terms of Eq. (10) from above, whereas _h_<sub>**x**</sub>+_l_<sub>**x**</sub> represents _a_(**x**)/2. Instead of _P_, the tensor cores return the value \(\widehat{P}\), which results from exact products of the half-precision coordinates and an accumulation of these products in fp32. The test of CertEx compares this value with a threshold: CertEx keeps a vector if and only if \(\widehat{P}\) satisfies

\(\widehat{P}\ge\theta(\mathbf{q}):=\frac{a(\mathbf{q})-U^2}{2}-\mu(\mathbf{q}),\) (12)

where the _margin_ \(\mu(\mathbf{q}):=\gamma(\overline{e_\mathbf{q}}M_n+\overline{n_\mathbf{q}}M_e+M_l)\) uses the database maxima _Mn_, _Me_, and _Ml_ of _n_**x**, _e_**x**, and |_l_**x**|. The proof of Proposition 3 uses every coordinate of the retina vectors, which we now define. We assume that the data are scaled once so that every lifted coordinate and every _a_(**x**)/2 lies in the normal range of half precision. This assumption loses no generality, because a common scale multiplies all distances by the same factor and therefore leaves the neighbors unchanged. The coordinates that carry the error terms are themselves stored in half precision and must still bound norms and errors from above. We therefore write fl(_v_) for the rounding of _v_ to the nearest half-precision number and up(_v_):=fl((1+2-10)_v_) for rounding up. Since rounding to nearest changes a value in the normal range by at most the relative 2-11, \(\mathrm{up}(v)\ge(1+2^{-10})(1-2^{-11})v>v\) for every _v\>_0. Although the norms inside up are computed in fp32, their relative error stays far below this margin. ## 3.5 Foveal Verification and Exactness

The fovea needs the threshold _U_ before the retina pass and the exact distances of the survivors after it. Before the pass, CertEx samples every _s_-th retina vector, for a stride _s_, and scores the sampled vectors by the same computed product \(\widehat{P}\) as the retina pass. Among them, the sampled vectors with the largest products become the _anchors_ A(**q**). The threshold _U_ is then the _k_-th smallest exact distance among the anchors. Because the anchors are at least _k_ distinct vectors of X, \(U\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\) holds for every query. After the pass, the fovea computes the exact distance of each survivor from the full-precision difference **q**-**x** and returns the _k_ smallest per query.

**Proposition 4** (Exactness)**.** _CertEx returns_ N_<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) _for every query_ **q**.

_Proof._ Every **x** with \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|\le U\) satisfies \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\le U\) by Proposition 2 and survives by Proposition 3. The retina is therefore a certified exclusion test. Since \(U\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\), Proposition 1 yields the claim.

The anchors, the rotation **V**, and the width _m_ therefore influence only the cost of CertEx. For instance, a loose threshold admits more survivors and more exact distances but cannot remove a true neighbor. To quantify this cost, Proposition 5 bounds the number of survivors. For this purpose, we write \(\rho(\mathbf{x}):=\|(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c})\|\) for the last coordinate of \(\ell(\mathbf{x})\), which is the norm of the component of **x**-**c** that is orthogonal to the rows of **V**. Similarly, we denote by \(\eta(\mathbf{q})\) the _slack_ that \(\mu(\mathbf{q})\) and the rounded-up coordinates add to the squared threshold, which is of the order of the unit roundoff times the squared norms.

**Proposition 5** (Survivor ball)**.** _Every vector that the retina keeps for the threshold U satisfies_ \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\le U^2+\eta(\mathbf{q})+4\rho(\mathbf{q})\rho(\mathbf{x})\).

_Proof._ The proof reuses the notation of the proof of Proposition 2. There, **u**=**q**-**c** and **v**=**x**-**c** split as **u**=**u**<sub>1</sub>+**u**<sub>2</sub> and **v**=**v**<sub>1</sub>+**v**<sub>2</sub>, where **u**<sub>1</sub>,**v**<sub>1</sub> lie in the row space of **V** and **u**<sub>2</sub>,**v**<sub>2</sub> are orthogonal to it. The norms of **u**<sub>2</sub> and **v**<sub>2</sub> are the last coordinates \(\rho(\mathbf{q})\) and \(\rho(\mathbf{x})\) of the lifted projections. The proof proceeds in three steps.

First, the retina keeps **x** only if its lifted distance is small. By the definition of the slack \(\eta(\mathbf{q})\), every kept vector satisfies

\(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2\le U^2+\eta(\mathbf{q}).\) (16)

Second, the squared distance exceeds the squared lifted distance by a term that involves only **u**<sub>2</sub> and **v**<sub>2</sub>. Eqs. (6), (5), and (4) give \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2=\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2+\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\) and \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2=\|\mathbf{u}_1-\mathbf{v}_1\|^2+(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2\). Subtracting the second equation from the first and expanding both<tbc>

<tbc>squares,

\(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|^2=\|\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{v}_2\|^2-(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|-\|\mathbf{v}_2\|)^2=\big(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|^2-2\langle\mathbf{u}_2,\mathbf{v}_2\rangle+\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\big)-\big(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|^2-2\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\|\mathbf{v}_2\|+\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\big)=2\big(\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\|\mathbf{v}_2\|-\langle\mathbf{u}_2,\mathbf{v}_2\rangle\big).\text{(17)}\)

Third, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds this excess. It gives \(-\langle\mathbf{u}_2,\mathbf{v}_2\rangle\le\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\|\mathbf{v}_2\|\), so that the right- hand side of Eq. (17) is at most \(4\|\mathbf{u}_2\|\|\mathbf{v}_2\|=4\rho(\mathbf{q})\rho(\mathbf{x})\). Adding this bound to Eq. (16) yields \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\le U^2+\eta(\mathbf{q})+4\rho(\mathbf{q})\rho(\mathbf{x})\), which is the claim.

The survivors therefore lie between two balls. Specifically, the inner ball has radius _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**), and its vectors always survive. In contrast, the outer ball is slightly larger, by an excess that grows with \(\rho(\mathbf{q})\) and \(\rho(\mathbf{x})\). Because the anchors are the best of every _s_-th vector, _U_ approximates the distance to the (_ks_)-th nearest neighbor. The number of survivors thus approaches _ks_ when the width captures most of the variance of the data. A batch of _B_ queries then costs _BN(m_+5) half-precision multiply-ads plus about _ks_ exact distances per query, whereas exhaustive search costs _BND_ full-precision multiply-ads and a selection among all _N_ candidates.

## 3.6 Certified Exclusion at Any Threshold

Certified exclusion holds for every threshold, so that CertEx answers any query that fixes its threshold in advance exactly and without the anchors. Specifically, Definition 1 and Proposition 3 hold for every \(U\ge 0\), so that the test of the retina is certified whatever threshold a query uses. The anchors of Section 3.5 have a different role: they choose the threshold _U_ when a query does not fix it. For instance, kNN search does not fix its threshold, because Proposition 1 requires \(U\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\) and the distance _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) becomes known only after the search. In contrast, a _range query_ with radius _r_ asks for all database vectors within _r_ of the query, so that its threshold is _r_ from the start. CertEx thus answers a range query by setting _U_:=_r_, without any anchors. Since the retina may also keep vectors farther than _r_, the fovea computes their exact distances and removes them. CertEx therefore returns exactly the vectors within _r_, by Propositions 2 and 3.

In particular, near-duplicate detection fixes its threshold in advance as well, because it asks for all pairs of database vectors whose distance is at most a given radius _r_. We call the set of these pairs the _similarity self-join_. The self-join therefore consists of the range queries of all database vectors against the database, which CertEx answers exactly as above. Because each pair appears in two of these range<tbc>

<tbc>queries, the retina pass evaluates only the pairs (**x**_<sub>i</sub>,_**x**_<sub>j</sub>_) with _i\<j_, so that each pair is tested once. In practice, the radius _r_ follows from the criterion of deduplication pipelines such as SemDeDup \[1\], which keep the pairs whose cosine similarity is at least \(\tau\). For unit vectors, such as normalized image embeddings, this criterion corresponds to the radius \(r=\sqrt{2-2\tau}\). Because the self-join is defined by a radius rather than by a number of neighbors, it places no limit on the number of duplicates per vector. In contrast, a kNN graph keeps at most _k_ neighbors of each vector and therefore misses every duplicate beyond the _k_-th neighbor.

## 4 Evaluation

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Datasets and encoders.

The evaluation covers sixteen descriptor, word, and image-embedding datasets that span dimension and scale ( 1). Specifically, SIFT1M, GIST1M, and the BIGANN prefixes up to 100M vectors \[33, 37\] contain SIFT \[42\] and GIST \[48\] descriptors, whereas Deep-image \[72\] and GloVe \[52\] contain 9.99M CNN descriptors and 1.18M word embeddings. Moreover, the ImageNet-1K datasets \[15, 57\] use 1.28M training images as the database and 10,000 validation images as queries, both embedded by seven vision encoders, which are vision transformers \[16\] of the CLIP \[56\], SigLIP \[73\], DINOv2 \[50\], and DINOv3 \[61\] families. In addition, a cross-modal workload queries the CLIP image embeddings with 10,000 CLIP text prompts of the 1,000 class names. At web scale, DataComp \[21\] contributes the CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings of 12.79M web image-text pairs with 10,000 image and caption queries.

#### Platform, metrics, and baselines.

Unless stated otherwise, every experiment runs on one NVIDIA H100 GPU with the kernels of CertEx written in Triton \[64\] on top of PyTorch \[51\]. Section 4.8 repeats four datasets on an A100, at 8.8\(\times\) to 11.8\(\times\) cuVS. Every experiment keeps the<tbc>

<tbc>database in device memory next to the retina, which adds 2(_m_+5) bytes per vector. Because the fovea reads only the survivors, the database could also reside in host memory. Throughput counts the queries per second over all queries with _k_=10 after a warm-up pass. For exactness, we recompute the squared distances of the returned neighbors by direct differences in fp64 and call a query exact when these sorted distances equal those of the true neighbors to a relative 10<sup>-12</sup>, which accepts ties among equidistant vectors and no other deviation. The true neighbors come from an fp64 search that is reranked by direct differences in fp64. We compare CertEx with six GPU baselines: the exhaustive search of NVIDIA cuVS \[47\] in fp32 at its fastest selection size, the same search in half precision with exact reranking, and the cuVS indexes IVF-Flat \[62\], IVF-PQ \[37\], IVF- RaBitQ \[22\], and CAGRA \[49\]. For a fair comparison, each baseline uses the best configuration of a grid, with exact reranking for the quantized indexes, as does CertEx with a few widths and anchor strides per dataset.

## 4.4 Vision Encoders

We next ask whether the retina stays selective on modern vision encoders (Figure 5). On all seven ImageNet encoders, the retina keeps few survivors, so that CertEx is exact for every query and faster than every baseline at 99.9% exact queries (Figure 5(a)). Moreover, a larger width tightens the bound, so that the survivors per query on DINOv2 [50] fall from 10.3k at _m_=507 to 671 at _m_=763 (Figure 5(b)).

Cross-modal queries further test exactness under a shift of the query distribution, because CLIP [56] text embeddings occupy a different region of the joint embedding space than the image embeddings [40]. Consequently, IVF- Flat [62] is the only index that reaches 99.9% exact text queries, whereas CertEx is exact for every text query at \(41\times\) its throughput (Figure 5(a), right), because certified exclusion does not depend on the query distribution.

We finally ask what exact neighbors change in deduplication and kNN classification (Figure 6 and Figure 7). For duplicate detection, the exact self-join of the 1.28M ImageNet [15] training images takes 1.5 to 2.5 seconds,<tbc>

## 4.7 Certified Screening in Inverted Lists

Inverted-file indexes restrict every query to the lists nearest to it and compute the distance to every vector of these lists in full precision, so that their cost grows linearly with the number of probed lists. Certified exclusion applies inside the probed lists without changing the candidates of a query. Specifically, screening the retina rows of the probed lists under a threshold from their anchors, followed by ordered verification, returns the exact _k_ nearest neighbors among the vectors of the probed lists. The answer of CertEx therefore equals the answer of an exhaustive scan of the same lists, and both reach the same recall. We evaluate this combination against IVF-Flat [62] of cuVS [47] on SIFT1M, BIGANN-10M, and ImageNet DINOv2 with _k_=10, 1,024 lists, and 1 to 500 probed lists on one H100.

The two methods share the centers of the lists, which cuVS trains, and every vector joins the list of its nearest center. CertEx stores the vectors in list order with one global projection, so that a routed kernel screens the queries that probe a list against the rows of that list only. Every list keeps 128 evenly spaced anchors. The threshold of a query is the _k_-th exact distance among the 128 anchors of its probed lists whose retina products are largest. Ordered verification then computes the exact distances of the 32 survivors of smallest certified bound and drops every survivor whose bound exceeds the resulting _k_-th distance. Exhaustive search over the probed lists in double precision confirms that CertEx is exact within the probed lists for 200 queries at every setting. The answers of the two methods coincide on every query of SIFT1M and DINOv2, whereas on the uint8 vectors of BIGANN-10M the lists of cuVS place some vectors<tbc>

<tbc>differently, so that the two answers differ at few probed lists while their recall stays within 0.02.

Figure 9 reports the throughput of both methods against the number of probed lists, with the recall@10 of CertEx at three settings on the top axis. The throughput of IVF- Flat falls in proportion to the probed lists, because it computes the distance to every vector of these lists. In contrast, CertEx verifies an almost constant number of vectors per query (100 to 244 on SIFT1M, 155 to 258 on BIGANN- 10M, and 129 to 147 on DINOv2), so that its throughput falls slowly. CertEx therefore overtakes IVF-Flat at 50 probed lists on SIFT1M and BIGANN-10M, where both reach recall 0.99, and at 10 probed lists on DINOv2, where both reach recall 0.978. At 200 probed lists, where the recall of CertEx exceeds 0.999, CertEx is 4.7, 3.6, and 23.7 times faster than IVF-Flat on the three datasets, and on DINOv2 it is 40.1 times faster at 500 probed lists.

At one to five probed lists, IVF-Flat is faster than CertEx, because it reads only a few thousand rows per query, whereas the anchor stage of CertEx costs 51 to 63 ms per 10,000 queries regardless of the probed lists. Certified exclusion therefore turns the exhaustive scan of the probed lists into a screen whose cost hardly depends on the number of probed lists, which matters at the high recall that applications sensitive to missed neighbors require. The retina of DINOv2 needs a wide projection, because the 768- dimensional embeddings spread their variance over many directions. For instance, at _m_=255 the survivors grow to 45,800 per query at 200 probed lists, and CertEx only matches IVF-Flat, whereas _m_=507 keeps them at about 1,000.

### 4.8 Exact Search on an A100

The certificate of CertEx assumes only half-precision products with fp32 accumulation \[10\], which the tensor cores of other GPUs provide as well. We therefore repeat the exact search of SIFT1M, GIST1M, GloVe, and BIGANN- 10M with the same code on an NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe GPU ( 2). The A100 runs as one MIG instance of the 7g.80gb profile, which provides 98 of its 108 streaming multiprocessors and its full memory. On this instance, CertEx searches the anchor strides 8, 16, and 32 at the widths around its H100 configuration. The baseline is the fastest configuration of the same cuVS \[47\] fp32 grid on the same instance.

On all four datasets, CertEx is exact for every query at \(8.8\times\) to \(11.8\times\) the throughput of the fastest cuVS fp32 configuration, against \(7.7\times\) to \(15.5\times\) on the H100. In addition, the boundary validation of Section 4.3 keeps every pair in all 24 runs. As on the H100, the largest speedup belongs to BIGANN-10M \[33\], the largest of the four datasets. Moving from the H100 to the A100, CertEx loses \(2.3\times\) to \(2.5\times\) of its throughput, whereas exhaustive search loses \(1.9\times\) on three datasets and \(2.75\times\) on the 960 dimensions of GIST1M. The speedup on GIST1M therefore rises from \(7.7\times\) to \(9.3\times\). Moreover, the fastest width changes on two datasets: GIST1M prefers _m_=379 instead of 507, and BIGANN-10M prefers _m_=59 instead of 123. Because the width affects only the cost, every width remains exact on both GPUs.

## 5 Conclusion

Exact kNN search for image retrieval, deduplication, and the memory of LLM agents has so far required either a full- precision distance to every vector or an index that gives up exactness. CertEx shows that exact search needs neither: a lifted lower bound with a certificate for its rounding error excludes almost every vector in one half-precision tensor- core pass without a false dismissal. On sixteen datasets of up to 100M vectors, CertEx is exact for every query at up to \(18.0\times\) the throughput of the fastest exhaustive GPU search. Exact search thus becomes a practical default for visual retrieval, deduplication, and representation evaluation.
